newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Indonesia buys meal, buyers await USDA report.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia buys meal, buyers await USDA report.

text.p: Indonesia locked up at least two cargoes of soymeal while the rest of the Southeast Asian grain and oilseeds trade sat on the fence to wait for the release of a critical USDA crop report next week, dealers said on Wednesday.

Indonesian buyers bought one Panamax-sized shipment of Argentine-origin soymeal for January/February shipment at a price around US$285/290 a tonne C&F and also purchased about 11,000 tonnes of Indian-origin meal for the same shipment period worth about $295/298 a tonne C&F, Singapore-based dealers said.
"Those deals were done very recently," a trader in a Western commodity house said.
"There's still open demand from Indonesia for February shipment of about 80,000 to 90,000 tonnes of soymeal," one trader in a U.S. commodity company added.
A Thai purchase about 10 days ago of around 50,000 tonnes of U.S.-origin soybeans was also done at about $298 a tonne C&F, dealers said.
"We should continue to see good export business in soybeans," another dealer said. "Corn, however, is like a bottomless pit as far as prices are concerned."

But the remaining grains and oilseeds trade in Southeast Asia was again quiet for the second week running as most buyers decided to wait for release of the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) crop report on November 12.
"Everything has slowed down ahead of that report," a trader in a European foodgrains company said.

Singapore-based dealers said buyers were expecting the U.S. corn crop may be within reach of 9.4 billion bushels, up from the USDA October forecast of 9.012 billion bushels. Prices may plunge further if the crop estimate heads up, dealers said.

"The numbers are creeping up to 9.4 billion bushels and that's causing the end-users to step aside. No one wants to stick their neck out and this will continue until next Tuesday," a trader in a U.S. commodity firm said.

"Buyers are greedy," declared a senior dealer in a European trading house, adding many are betting that prices will head lower on a bearish USDA crop report. "No business is being done. Sentiment is very bearish."
The December corn futures contract on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) sank to a fresh 14-month session low on Tuesday of $2.57-3/4 a bushel before closing at $2.58-1/2 a bushel.
One analyst predicted that if the USDA corn report failed to reach 9.4 billion bushels, buyers may begin jumping into the market on the belief that prices have bottomed out.
"If the USDA sticks to its figure, you'll see some buyers jumping in to get some cover because they believe prices will begin moving up again," the analyst said.

The situation in corn was mirrored in wheat, where buyers were also watching closely contract lows in the CBOT set on Tuesday. The new low for March wheat is $3.63-1/2 a bushel, down from the previous low on Friday of $3.65-1/2 a bushel.
"Wheat buying has dried up. Nothing has been done over the past week," one trader said.
Prices in Southeast Asia took their cue from the U.S. and also fell, traders said.

U.S. corn was quoted by regional traders at $139/$142 a tonne C&F Southeast Asia destinations on a Panamax vessel for January/February shipment, down from $147/$150 last week and a price of up to $160 a tonne C&F at the beginning of October.
U.S. soybeans were priced around $290 a tonne C&F for January/February shipment against $295/$296 last week.

Indian-origin soymeal was quoted at around $295 a tonne C&F for January/February shipment from last week's $297/$306. It was priced at around $316/$318 a tonne C&F for November/December shipment in early October.

U.S. low-protein soymeal was fetching a quote of $280/$281 a tonne C&F for January/February shipment against $282/$283 the previous week, dealers said. It was seen as high as $309 a tonne C&F for November/December shipment in early October.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
